idRows.title: VoroTypes: automated enumeration of Voronoi cell topologies for structural identification of complex crystals in atomistic simulations
idRows.summary: VoroTypes enumerates, for an arbitrary crystal structure, the complete family of Voronoi cell topologies that can arise under small generic perturbations of atomic positions, and exports it as a topological filter for the VoroTop framework. This extends per-atom structural identification in molecular dynamics simulations, previously limited to a handful of simple reference structures, to complex crystals such as Frank--Kasper and Laves phases, with per-sublattice resolution. The package takes a standard crystallographic description (a CIF or POSCAR file) as input, applies exact symmetry reduction and validity pruning to accelerate the enumeration, and produces filters that load directly into the standalone VoroTop program or into OVITO. A library of pre-computed filters covers over a thousand structures from the Materials Project.

idRows.title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells
idRows.summary: While graphene/n-type silicon (Gr/n-Si) and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si solar cells offer a cost-effective alternative to conventional photovoltaics, achieving simultaneous high power conversion efficiency (PCE) and long-term environmental stability remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report the synergistic enhancement of both performance and stability in a planar trilayer PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si Schottky junction architecture. By systematically benchmarking this hybrid device against pristine Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells fabricated on untextured substrates, we isolate the fundamental optoelectronic and barrier functions of the carbon lattice. Comprehensive analyses reveal that the PEDOT:PSS layer simultaneously functions as an anti-reflection coating, a moderate p-type dopant for the underlying graphene, and a conductivity enhancer, collectively optimizing interfacial charge transport. Consequently, the trilayer device achieves a PCE of 8.52%, markedly outperforming the pristine Gr/n-Si reference cell (4.56%). Crucially, the atomic impermeability of the graphene sheet serves as a robust environmental barrier. While bare PEDOT:PSS/n-Si junctions retained only ~29% of their initial efficiency after 75 days of ambient exposure, graphene shields the active junction from moisture-induced degradation of the hygroscopic PEDOT:PSS overlayer. This enables the trilayer device to retain approximately 90% of its initial efficiency over the same 75-day period. The complementary roles of graphene as both a highly crystalline charge transport interface and an impermeable protective barrier establish a highly effective strategy for engineering high-efficiency, environmentally stable hybrid photovoltaics.

idRows.title: Imaging defects in two-dimensional crystals by convergent beam electron diffraction
idRows.summary: Convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED), recently demonstrated on two-dimensional (2D) materials, offers a number of interesting applications such as imaging atomic in- and out-of plane shifts, interlayer distances, and individual adsorbates. In this study, we show how CBED allows for atomic-precision imaging of individual defects in 2D materials using one single-shot intensity measurement. In combination with structural calculations using density functional theory, we present simulated CBED patterns for various defects in graphene, each of which exhibits a unique fingerprint distribution. We also show how atomic positions, including the individual atomic defects in graphene, can be reconstructed by iterative phase retrieval from a single CBED pattern.

idRows.title: Large in-plane optical anisotropy in epitaxial CrN(113) films
idRows.summary: CrN, a transition-metal nitride crystallizing in the cubic rocksalt structure, exhibits a unique combination of mechanical robustness, semiconducting behavior, and thermoelectric functionality. To date, however, CrN has been synthesized primarily as polycrystalline material or as epitaxial films grown along high-symmetry orientations such as (001) and (111). Here, we prepare epitaxial CrN(113) films on AlN(11\bar{2}2) templates by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy. The low-symmetry interface and highly direction dependent lattice mismatch are expected to modify the physical properties of CrN relative to the bulk material. Indeed, variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry in the photon-energy range from 1.25 to 5 eV reveals a surprisingly strong polarization dependence of the optical response despite the nearly strain-free cubic crystal structure of the films. The pseudo-optical constants n and k differ by more than 10% for orthogonal in-plane polarizations throughout the investigated spectral range. We evaluate possible origins of this effect and conclude that it most likely arises from anisotropic surface morphology of CrN(113), which creates a metasurface acting as a subwavelength grating in the strongly absorbing regime.

idRows.title: Localization induced by Sinai disorder in mass-exchange models
idRows.summary: We introduce a conservative continuous-mass-exchange model with quenched disorder in the splitting laws on the bonds of a finite segment. Although the dynamics is generically irreversible, its stationary mean mass profile remarkably turns out to be exactly solvable through an associated birth-and-death chain and has a Gibbs representation in terms of a simple random-walk potential. If $N$ is the number of bonds and $β$ measures the strength of disorder, the parameter $β\sqrt N$ separates an asymptotically flat profile, a Brownian crossover, and a profile localized near the global minimum. We characterize the fluctuations of macroscopic masses and identify arcsine laws for the localization centre, the competition between left and right valleys, and the disorder-averaged mass measure. Furthermore, for the extremal masses, we discuss the emergent limiting random variable in terms of the literature linking finite RW paths seen from its minimum to infinite-horizon walks conditioned to stay positive. Finally, in proximity of the localization transition point $β=0$, we show that the inverse participation ratio for the extremal masses give rises to a scaling with decay of order $k^{-3/2}$ consistent with the scaling limit of the latter conditioned walk. In the same limit, the inverse participation ratio shows a scaling form.

idRows.title: Edge state reconstruction in proximitized graphene and its probe using RKKY interaction
idRows.summary: Proximity induced spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in graphene emerges when it is placed on a substrate, breaking sublattice symmetry and giving rise to staggered intrinsic SOC together with Rashba spin-orbit coupling. In zigzag graphene nanoribbons, this staggered SOC produces pseudohelical edge states exhibiting sublattice-locked rather than spin-locked helicity. We investigate the effect of a finite on-site potential, restricted to the edges of the ribbon, on these edge states. We find the inter-valley edge states undergo reconstruction and become purely intra-valley, exhibiting both spin and valley polarization. The charge conductance calculations fail to capture this reconstruction, since the number of transmitted channels remains unchanged. We show that the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) magnetic exchange interaction, between two magnetic impurities situated on the ribbon edge can be used to probe the shifted band dispersion, for both the uniform and staggered spin-orbit coupling. In the presence of strong intrinsic and Rashba SOC, the RKKY interaction becomes fully anisotropic. Both sublattice staggering and edge potential-induced reconstruction lead to distinct features in the RKKY interaction. We show that the RKKY interaction terms acquire faster oscillations as a function of the spatial separation between two magnetic impurities, in response to the edge state reconstruction, establishing it as an effective probe of the edge states. Additionally, the significant mismatch in the amplitudes of the DM term corresponding to the uniform and staggered SOC, can also act as a probe of the type of SOC.

idRows.title: Broadband radio-frequency TEM specimen holders for in situ biasing excitation and 100-ps-scale electron beam control
idRows.summary: Broadband electrical excitation inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) is required to investigate electrically driven nanodevices at their actual operating frequencies and to develop fully electrical time-resolved experiments at a sub-nanosecond range. Here, we report the performances of homemade two- and four-channel radio-frequency (RF) TEM specimen holders based on a hybrid architecture combining coaxial transmission lines with miniaturized impedance-controlled printed circuit boards (PCB). Removable mechanical contacts provide direct electrical connection to interchangeable TEM chips without wire bonding. Vector network analyzer measurements demonstrate broadband transmission through the complete electrical path up to the specimen. With a representative TEM chip, the two-channel holder exhibits a -3 dB bandwidth of 7.9 GHz, while insertion losses remain below 12 dB up to 18 GHz. The same RF holder architecture was used to drive a miniaturized electrostatic electron-beam deflector. The measured temporal response indicates that the holder deflector assembly remains compatible with electrical pulse durations approaching 100 ps, with the shortest accessible times presently limited by the available waveform generator. High-resolution TEM imaging with a 200 ps probe window does not show detectable degradation of spatial resolution, while off-axis electron holography is successfully performed for probe durations down to 0.5 ns under conditions representative of operando measurements. These results establish a versatile broadband platform combining GHz electrical excitation and sub-nanosecond electron-beam control. The dual-stage configuration of our Hitachi HF3300 microscope further provides the basis for a future fully electrical pump-probe TEM approach using independently driven RF holders for specimen excitation and electron-probe control.

idRows.title: Spatiotemporally correlated activity regulation of random-organizing hyperuniform states
idRows.summary: Center-of-mass (COM) conservation has been widely accepted as an important mechanism for generating nonequilibrium dynamic hyperuniform states with vanishing long-wavelength density fluctuations, but whether it is sufficient for hyperuniformity remains unclear. Here, using particle simulations and a linear fluctuating theory, we show that spatiotemporally correlated activity regulation can destroy hyperuniformity while preserving COM conservation. We construct a binary mixture in which the local density of independently evolving driver particles regulates the activity of regulated particles following COM-conserving biased random organization. This counterexample demonstrates that hyperuniformity depends on the spatial and temporal correlations of activity as well as the conservation laws governing particle displacements. Our findings clarify the limits of COM conservation as a route to hyperuniformity and highlight the importance of controlling activity correlations in the design of nonequilibrium multihyperuniform mixtures.

idRows.title: Non-equilibrium Muon Dynamics Imitating Fractional Spin Excitations in a Quantum Spin Chain
idRows.summary: Fractional spin excitations in low-dimensional and frustrated magnets are commonly associated with sporadic spin fluctuations, as observed in quantum spin liquids, spin ices, and other complex magnetic states. In this study, we investigate the spin dynamics in the amplitude-modulated magnetic ground state of AgCuVO$_4$, a spin-1/2 chain compound with competing intrachain interactions, by muon spectroscopy. Our data reveal a Gaussian decay of muon polarization that remains remarkably resilient against applied magnetic fields---a behavior often interpreted as evidence of emergent sporadic spin dynamics. However, density functional theory calculations of muon stopping sites and their quadrupolar level-crossing resonance spectra suggest an alternative mechanism: a two-state model where the muon randomly hops between two nearby sites, eventually equilibrating across both on a microsecond timescale via quantum delocalization. These findings provide a microscopic explanation for the field-resilient muon polarization and indicate that such behavior may not always stem from intrinsic spin fluctuations, but can also arise from non-equilibrium muon dynamics.

idRows.title: Coherent and Incoherent Time-Resolved Diffuse Scattering Intensity from First Principles
idRows.summary: Time-resolved diffuse scattering from X-ray free-electron lasers and ultrafast electron diffraction gives access to the nonequilibrium lattice dynamics of photoexcited solids in reciprocal space. Existing interpretations have often relied on simplified models. Here we present a first-principles formulation of the time-dependent first-order diffuse intensity in which coherent and incoherent contributions emerge on equal footing. By assuming the probe-pulse coherence time to be longer than the characteristic electronic timescales, but shorter than those of the ionic motion, we work in the density-matrix formalism and derive equations of motion for the displacement-displacement correlators in a basis of instantaneous, out-of-equilibrium Born-Oppenheimer normal modes. We show how the incoherent contribution, governed by the phonon occupations, and a coherent contribution, governed by the anomalous phonon correlators, emerge. The non-trivial coherent dynamics is shown to be induced both by the photoinduced phonon-frequency shift and by electron-phonon scattering off the nonequilibrium carrier distribution. We implement the resulting equations using Wannier interpolation in the \textsc{EPI}q code and apply them to photoexcited germanium. The calculated diffuse intensity reproduces both the oscillation frequencies and the rising incoherent background observed experimentally, opening the way to a systematic interpretation of time-resolved diffuse scattering in ultrafast experiments.

idRows.title: Interpretable machine learning of formation energies and band gaps in hybrid perovskites through SHAP analysis and SISSO modelling
idRows.summary: Accurate and interpretable property prediction is essential for exploring hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites. Here, we combine machine-learning screening with SHAP analysis and SISSO descriptor discovery. Using 4,456 compounds, optimized XGBoost models achieved test-set $R^2$ values of 0.99 for formation energy and 0.93 for band gap and were applied to over 180,000 candidates. Comparison across approximately 17,000 common compounds revealed broadly overlapping distributions from XGBoost and CGCNN but substantially lower predictions from UPET, suggesting potential limitations in its transferability to hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites. SHAP analysis and correlation-based pruning retained eight primary features for each property, from which SISSO derived expressions comprising four nonlinear descriptors. These expressions couple molecular and inorganic properties for formation energy and emphasize relative atomic sizes and B-site characteristics for band gap. This framework supports efficient candidate prioritization and interpretable analysis of learned structures-property relationships in hybrid perovskites.

idRows.title: Bond-informed search for ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys
idRows.summary: Ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) control their local structure and influence a broad range of mechanical and thermodynamic properties. Yet they are notoriously difficult to identify. Locating low-energy ordered candidates requires exploring a configurational space that grows combinatorially with the number of elements, and Monte Carlo searches driven by density-functional theory (DFT) need a new electronic-structure calculation at every trial step. Here we introduce MECx (Minimum Energy Configuration eXplorer), a framework that guides Monte Carlo searches with a surrogate energy model trained on configurations stratified in bond-count space. Applied to ternary, quaternary, and quinary BCC alloys using compact training sets of 100 DFT-labeled configurations, MECx identifies ordered configurations with lower energies than those found by direct DFT-based Monte Carlo within practical computational limits. These configurations exhibit distinct pair-specific ordering, including B2- and B32-like motifs, and undergo progressive disordering as temperature increases. The MPEA-trained models also transfer to selected binary subsystems without retraining. The resulting ordered configurations agree with those obtained by direct DFT-based Monte Carlo and produce experimentally distinguishable superlattice reflections in simulated neutron diffraction patterns.

idRows.title: Modified anisotropy and distinct phase diagrams in the nearly isotropic $S=1$ triangular-lattice antiferromagnet $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$
idRows.summary: The triangular-lattice antiferromagnet serves as a benchmark platform for realizing exotic quantum phases, in which magnetic anisotropy plays an essential role. In this work, we report modified magnetic anisotropy and phase diagrams in the nearly isotropic $S=1$ triangular-lattice antiferromagnet $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$, compared with those of its isostructural analog $\mathrm{K_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. The magnetic susceptibility of $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$ exhibits an easy-axis anisotropy with $g_c > g_{ab}$, opposite to the easy-plane anisotropy observed in $\mathrm{K_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. The single Néel transition observed at zero field splits into two transitions at around 10~T, and a magnetization plateau is observed between 21~T and 37~T for both out-of-plane ($H\parallel c$) and in-plane ($H\parallel ab$) field directions in $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. We construct magnetic phase diagrams that are distinct between $\mathrm{Rb_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$ and $\mathrm{K_2Ni(SeO_3)_2}$. These findings highlight the sensitivity of field-induced magnetic phase behavior to anisotropy in nearly isotropic triangular-lattice antiferromagnets.

idRows.title: Discontinuous-Property Mechanical Metamaterials: A Framework for Discontinuous Lattice Dynamics
idRows.summary: Discontinuity, as the extreme limit of nonlinearity, is common in macroscopic continuum systems. This work introduces discontinuous-property mechanical metamaterials (DPMMs) as a prototype for establishing a geometric-mechanics framework for discontinuous lattice systems. We extend band theory to systems with complementary constraints through geometric regularization and analyze modal discontinuities. By analyzing its static, modal, and transient responses, we validated discontinuous stiffness and Poisson's ratio, alongside intense nonlinear wave mixing and mode conversion. A proof-of-concept experiment demonstrates the practical feasibility of implementing DPMMs. This work characterizes discontinuous lattice systems through the intuitive DPMM concept and provides a practical framework to harness sharp transitions in mechanical metamaterials for nonlinear wave manipulation.

idRows.title: Theory of Dispersion and Exchange Interactions Subjected to Surface Roughness in Application to Signal Transmission through a Nanoswitch
idRows.summary: We present the theoretical description of a resistive nanoswitch designated for a change-over between the two operation modes by calculating the electri elastic, dispersion (van der Waals and Casimir), and also exchange repulsive forces in its configuration with an account of surface roughness. The dispersion forces are described by means of the Lifshitz theory and, at the shortest separations between the interacting bodies, where this theory is inapplicable, by the method of additive summation of the interatomic potentials corrected for the role of the effects of nonadditivity. The exchange repulsion is also found by a summation of the interatomic potentials and using the proximity force approximation. It is shown that the nanoswitch possesses the equilibrium closest separation between a cantilever tip and a ground plate calculated as a function of the actuation voltage and operates in a cyclic manner with no pull-in when this voltage is switched on and off. We have found the tunnel current between a cantilever tip and a plate and investigated distortions appearing in the signal transmitted through a nanoswitch. According to our results, the amplitude distortions arising in the low-frequency information signal can be made sufficiently small by increasing a difference between the amplitudes of the carrier and information signals. Possible applications of the obtained results are discussed.

idRows.title: Directed impulsive molecular dynamics reveal energy-routing pathways of bond cleavage in TATB
idRows.summary: Responses of energetic materials to external stimuli involve more than uniform thermalization. Understanding directional energy redistribution is essential for structural and ignition design. Here, we use TATB as an example to construct a vibrationally faithful machine-learning potential from only 4,630 configurations. To resolve the elusive nonequilibrium energy flow, we develop directed impulsive molecular dynamics, a statistically controlled protocol that repeatedly deposits equal kinetic energy along selected vibrational modes. By amplifying mode-specific responses while tracking the ensuing nonequilibrium evolution, this approach turns energy redistribution into a directly traceable routing process. We find that initial bond cleavage depends strongly on the initially excited mode, rather than being determined by bond-cleavage barriers alone. Specifically, modes that readily trigger reaction efficiently channel energy towards a bond cleavage coordinate, whereas modes that are less effective at inducing break divert energy into soft-like modes or trap it in modes from which energy flow is inefficient.

idRows.title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses
idRows.summary: Artificial visual synapses combine sensing, memory and processing in a single device, but most of them need an external voltage to read the synaptic weight and light is generally able to strengthen the weight rather than to weaken it. We report here Se/ZnMgO thin film photodiodes in which the photocurrent at zero bias writes and reads the synaptic weight, with a direction of change set by the photon energy alone. At equal photon flux, 365 nm pulses increase the photocurrent by 38 % while 455 nm pulses decrease it, and the depression reaching 30 % at higher flux, with up to 19 distinguishable levels per branch and no electrical energy spent. Spectrally resolved light soaking shows that short wavelengths potentiate while low-energy light erases. The interesting property is therefore the photon energy-dependent competition between potentiation and depression, the crossover being set by the defect population of the interface. Optical simulations show that both wavelengths are absorbed within the first tens of nanometres of Se, and the stored state is erased by a reverse bias in a voltage-dependent way and by sub-gap light, which indicates that potentiation corresponds to interface defects filled with electrons, in agreement with drift-diffusion simulations. The devices also show relearning, their response is modulated by bending on flexible substrates, and a network built from the measured weight updates reaches 89 % accuracy on handwritten digit recognition without noise and 85 % with the measured noise, against 97.5 % for floating-point weights.

idRows.title: Quantum instanton approach to metastable collective spin systems: Numerical implementation and applications
idRows.summary: Driven-dissipative collective spin systems can host several long-lived metastable states; rare switching between them governs slow relaxation and first-order dissipative phase transitions associated with changes in the dominant stationary state. In the companion Letter [arXiv:2604.15091], we introduced a quantum instanton framework based on exact quasiprobability dynamics to describe this switching and illustrated it with a minimal model possessing a simplifying symmetry. Here we develop its numerical implementation, combining collocation and shooting methods, and apply it to two microscopically motivated systems: the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model with purely collective dissipation and the cooperative resonance fluorescence with collective and local dissipation. By determining the leading exponential scaling of switching rates between metastable attractors, we predict the stationary magnetization, the first-order dissipative phase-transition point, and the exponential scaling of slow relaxation rates. These predictions agree with quantum master-equation calculations and an exact analytical result for the second model without dephasing. We also examine how the choice of quasiprobability representation affects numerical convergence and find that the alternative semiclassical Wigner approach, based on Gaussian truncation, has varying accuracy across models and parameter regimes. These results substantiate the framework's applicability to experimentally relevant collective spin systems with both collective and local dissipation.

idRows.title: Casimir forces on suspended thin dielectric membranes covered with graphene
idRows.summary: We investigate the Casimir force on thin suspended dielectric layers covered with graphene, both theoretically and experimentally. Thermal effects of the Casimir force on graphene occur at separations significantly smaller compared to ordinary metals and dielectrics. At such small separations, the Casimir force is sufficiently strong to be measured experimentally. However, the presence of substrates to support the graphene significantly reduces the enhancement. We show theoretically that replacing the solid substrate beneath graphene with a thin dielectric membrane partially restores this strong thermal dependence. One of the interacting objects is a solid gold plate. The other object is a suspended dielectric membrane made of either 15 nm of silicon oxide or 13 nm silicon nitride, covered with graphene. At a separation of $\sim$500 nm, theoretical predictions yield changes in the Casimir pressure of up to 54 % and 40 % for silicon oxide and silicon nitride, respectively, when the temperature is increased from 10 K to 294 K. Measurements were performed for graphene on a suspended silicon nitride membrane at room temperature, using a gold-coated sphere attached to a cantilever as the force sensor. The measured force gradient is consistent with the theoretical prediction, although the thermal dependence could not be resolved, in part because of uncertainties in the optical properties of silicon nitride. Replacing a bulk substrate with a thin dielectric membrane covered with graphene provides a substantial reduction of the Casimir force, which may facilitate the stable operation of neutral nanomechanical elements at small separations.

idRows.title: Diffusion-Induced Stabilization of Nonreciprocal Wealth Dynamics
idRows.summary: We study the stability of equal wealth shares in a spatial model combining local sharing, global redistribution, and random nonreciprocal interactions. On a two-dimensional square lattice in the infinite-system limit, the effect of local sharing depends on whether the influence of one site on another tends to have the same or opposite sign as the reverse influence. When these influences are nonnegatively correlated, diffusion reduces the redistribution required for stability, but a positive rate remains necessary. Negative correlations instead allow stability without redistribution, with the largest stability margin at finite diffusion and a return toward marginal stability at strong diffusion. This nonmonotonicity reflects a competition between spatial smoothing and the weakening of the stabilizing contribution of reciprocal anticorrelations. Equal shares can even remain stable under wealth-concentrating transfers, but only within an intermediate range of diffusion strengths.

idRows.title: Operator-Space Entanglement Entropy in Random Fermionic Gaussian Dynamics
idRows.summary: We study the von Neumann operator-space entanglement entropy (OSEE) of initial product operators evolved under random gaussian dynamics, as modeled by a Brownian SYK$_2$ model. By exploiting a mapping to a domain-wall melting problem, we derive an exact expression for the time-dependent bipartite OSEE in the thermodynamic limit, and obtain an analytic characterization of the corresponding gaussian Page curve emerging at late times. Our results build on recent work on the entanglement dynamics in the all-to-all quantum simple exclusion process, leveraging tools from RMT, including the Coulomb-gas approach and a mapping to the free Jacobi process. Finally, based on our results, we discuss the possibility of relating the OSEE with non-gaussianity measures in the Heisenberg picture.

idRows.title: Flat-band ferrimagnetism in the edge-centered honeycomb antiferromagnet: From harmonic flat magnon to broad continuum
idRows.summary: One of the most striking aspects of a flat band is not merely its lack of dispersion, but that it reduces the single-particle kinetic energy to a very small scale, allowing interaction effects to become the dominant energy scale in the low-energy physics. This picture has underpinned concepts such as flat-band ferromagnetism, flat-band superconductivity, and localized magnons. A more fundamental question, however, remains. Flat bands belong to the language of single-particle or linear-spin-wave physics; whether they survive as protected sharp excitations in a genuine many-body quantum magnet, or merely provide a skeleton of spectral weight left by the noninteracting picture, remains unclear. We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the edge-centered honeycomb lattice to examine this question. In contrast to flat bands in geometrically frustrated magnets such as kagome, this lattice has a 2:3 sublattice imbalance that renders the intersublattice coupling matrix rectangular, whose null space gives rise to a flat band at the single-particle level. The same imbalance stabilizes a ferrimagnetic ground state through the Lieb--Mattis theorem and leads to an edge-site-localized flat magnon in linear spin-wave theory. Combining linear spin-wave theory, sign-problem-free stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, and stochastic analytic continuation, we find that quantum fluctuations transform this harmonic flat mode into a broad continuum whose centroid is about 1.55J and nearly dispersionless along the high-symmetry path. Sublattice imbalance thus offers an unfrustrated route that unifies flat bands and ferrimagnetism, and suggests that flat-band geometry organizes many-body spectral weight rather than giving rise to a protected quasiparticle.

idRows.title: Indirect Control of Buried CoB Spin Textures via C$_{60}$-Induced Modification of Ir Spin-Orbit Coupling
idRows.summary: Understanding how organic materials modulate magnetic structure is a central challenge in organic spintronics. Here, we demonstrate that C$_{60}$ molecular films exert a pronounced and quantifiable influence on the buried magnetic spin texture in Pt/CoB/Ir based multilayer systems hosting interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI). Using Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, the magnetic domain behaviour in field-free and in-situ field environments is measured. In Fresnel mode, we reveal a reduction in magnetic domain periodicity upon C$_{60}$ deposition. Then, using pixelated 4D-STEM differential phase contrast mode, we establish that this modification arises from a substantial enhancement of effective magnetic anisotropy and interfacial DMI strength. Coupled with bulk magnetometry and micromagnetic simulations, we propose a mechanism based on spin-orbit coupling at the C$_{60}$/Ir interface which modifies the iDMI and drives a contraction of spin texture density throughout the multilayer stack. These findings extend the impact of organic molecular capping films as effective and accessible routes for engineering spin textures to buried magnetic multilayer systems, with direct implications for the design of next-generation spintronic and neuromorphic devices.

idRows.title: Critical Ising Model on the Periodic Cubic Lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^{3}$
idRows.summary: We investigate the critical behaviour of the nearest-neighbour Ising model on the three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^{3}$, and we present a companion set of Monte Carlo simulations. After recalling the rigorous results on the continuity of the spontaneous magnetization in $d=3$ and the triviality of the scaling limit in $d\ge 4$, we compile modern high-precision estimates of the 3D Ising critical exponents and verify the scaling relations that connect them. We then describe numerical measurements of the Binder cumulant, the magnetic susceptibility, the specific heat, the two-point correlation function, and the finite-size scaling of the magnetization. We discuss the systematic uncertainties that affect the extraction of the exponent ratios $γ/ν$ and $α/ν$, and we emphasize that an exponential fit of the correlation function is not appropriate at the critical point, where the decay is algebraic.

idRows.title: Pairing-channel reconstruction by Ising spin-orbit coupling in a multiorbital triangular-lattice model
idRows.summary: Ising spin-orbit coupling (SOC) is widely known for locking electronic spins and protecting superconductivity against in-plane paramagnetic pair breaking. Here we show that, in a correlated multiorbital system, Ising SOC can play a qualitatively different role: it reconstructs the hierarchy of spin-fluctuation-mediated pairing channels by reshaping the low-energy Fermi surfaces, orbital-spin coherence factors, and momentum-resolved scattering phase space. We study a noncentrosymmetric two-orbital triangular-lattice model with Rashba SOC, Ising SOC, and onsite SOC. We solve the pairing problem within a multiorbital random-phase-approximation framework. In the single-orbital limit, an $E$-representation state with a dominant $S_z=0$ component emerges only at relatively strong Ising SOC. Orbital degrees of freedom facilitate the stabilization of this pairing state at a smaller nominal Ising SOC strength and generate a broad competition between $E$ and $A_1$ pairing channels. The $E$ state can maintain the same $S_z=0$ triplet character, whereas the $A_1$ state becomes a fully gapped sign-changing $\splusminus$ superconductor. The latter also realizes a topologically nontrivial phase in the time-reversal-invariant weak-pairing regime, with a nonzero $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index, Wilson-loop spectral flow, and boundary modes. Its topology is not carried by a single orbital pairing component, but emerges cooperatively from the dominant intra- and inter-orbital pairing components. These results establish a microscopic route by which Ising SOC and orbital hybridization can reconstruct interaction-driven superconductivity, producing both Ising-triplet and topological singlet-dominated phases in correlated non-centrosymmetric systems.

idRows.title: Phase coexistence and nucleation of aging condensates
idRows.summary: Biomolecular condensates form by phase separation and often age over time by transitioning from liquid-like droplets to solid-like states. To capture the fundamental behavior of aging condensates, we connect the Flory-Huggins model of phase separation with the trap model of aging dynamics. This combined model yields a rich phase diagram, including a regime of metastable coexisting liquids. Interestingly, the dense metastable liquid serves as an intermediate state in the nucleation pathway of the glass, which thus nucleates in two steps. Our results are generic, since they follow from a basic free-energy structure, providing a unified foundation for describing the thermodynamics and kinetics of aging biomolecular condensates.

idRows.title: Difference between pair creation and anomaly matching: Nontrivial aspects of invertible symmetries and defects in $SU(N)$ models
idRows.summary: We study the connection between the $SU(N)_{K}$ Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) model and $SU(N)_{K'}$ WZW model, enforcing the $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ symmetries. The fundamental underlying structures are the (half-)integer spin simple currents in the topological quantum field theories and anomaly matching conditions in conformal field theories. For the (half-)integer spin simple current condition, we obtain the generalized pairing condition $K= \pm R^{2}K' (\text{mod}.N)$ with $\text{gcd}(R,N)=1$. On the other hand, the anomaly matching condition results in the weaker condition $K= \pm RUK' (\text{mod}.N)$ with $\text{gcd}(R,N)=\text{gcd}(U,N)=1$. The preservation law of the $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ defects and symmetries is compatible only with the pairing condition.
